biography.text: This focused dossier studies one part of Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Jābir ibn Sinān al-Battānī's astronomical work: the solar parameters reported in his zīj. Benno van Dalen's Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers entry, hosted by ISMI, places his observations at Raqqa and records the surviving transmission of the Ṣābiʾ Zīj. It does not attempt a full biography or harmonize variant life dates beyond that reference's reported bounds.
gaps: Compare the Arabic biographical notices and the manuscript evidence behind disputed life dates, family history, and observatory chronology.
Expand the dossier to separate investigations of eclipses, lunar theory, geography, instruments, and the zīj's tables.

timeline.text: Mozaffari places the solar observation year in the Yazdigird calendar year 251, corresponding to 15 April 882–14 April 883, and says the observations took place after 882 CE. Van Dalen reports a broader Raqqa observing period of 877–918. These dates describe reported observations, not the composition date of the whole zīj or the date of its surviving Escorial copy.
gaps: Check the dated observations and era conversion directly against Nallino's Latin and Arabic text and the Escorial witness.
Establish the composition history and relationship of the two editions mentioned by Ibn al-Nadīm without treating the surviving manuscript date as the work's date.

fields.text: The zīj reports a Ptolemaic solar-model eccentricity of 2;4,45 parts when the deferent radius is 60, and a tropical-year value of 365;14,26 days. Converting the latter's sexagesimal day fraction gives 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes, 24 seconds. The historical eccentricity belongs to the geocentric eccentric-circle model; it is not the modern Keplerian eccentricity of Earth's orbit. A separate calculation using e/R=2;4,45/60 gives a maximum equation near 1°59′9.1″, close to the rounded 1°59′10″ value reported in the later table tradition. This arithmetic check is explanatory, not a fresh reading of the Arabic witness.
gaps: Collate the Arabic solar chapters in Nallino, Pars III, pp. 64–73, against the scan and record an exact passage locator; do not transfer Pars I's Latin pp. 43–48 locator to the Arabic volume.
Read Nallino, Pars I, chapter 28, printed pp. 43–48, and commentary pp. 212–221, and compare them with the Arabic text and apparatus.

Resolve why Van Dalen reports qmax=1;59,10° while an independent arcsin(e/60) computation from e=2;4,45 yields 1;59,9.08°; check historical rounding, input precision, and the derivation described in chapter 28.
Check the table of the equation of centre in Nallino, Pars II, pp. 78–83, column by column against the reported parameter.
Determine precisely how Nallino and later authors derive the year value from the text and distinguish a direct observation from a derived table parameter.
Audit the model's observational method and error sources before evaluating accuracy or priority.

legacy.text: Nothaft identifies the Toledan Tables' maximum solar equation of 1;59,10° as implying the eccentricity 2;4,45 associated with al-Battānī. This supports a specific reception trail for a parameter in Latin astronomical tables. Van Dalen separately documents later readers and translators of the zīj. Neither fact makes the historical geocentric model identical to modern astronomy or proves direct borrowing in every later work that uses a similar value.
gaps: Trace the table value through the manuscripts and textual versions of the Toledan Tables and test whether the source attribution is explicit in each witness.
Investigate the zīj's Arabic, Castilian, Hebrew, and Latin transmission as separate documentary chains.
Do not turn later claims about Copernicus, Tycho, or European science into priority or causal claims without passage-level evidence.

Printed p. 329 note 3 reports e=2;4,45, qmax=1;59,10, tropical year 365;14,26 days, and observations after 882. sources.title: Ptolemaic Tradition and Islamic Innovation: The Astronomical Tables of Kūshyār ibn Labbān
sources.authorOrInstitution: Benno van Dalen, Ptolemaeus Arabus et Latinus, Texts 2, Brepols
sources.notes: Read the commentary on the solar equation and its notes. Van Dalen reports that al-Battānī explains his derivation of e=2;4,45 in Chapter 28 and locates this in Nallino Pars III, Arabic pp. 64–73, alongside the Latin translation in Pars I, pp. 43–48 and commentary pp. 212–221. He reports qmax=1;59,10° from accurate calculation. This is secondary scholarship and introduces a discrepancy with the dossier's independent calculation (1;59,9.08°); the discrepancy remains open pending direct source and formula review. Open access, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

works.subject: Ptolemaic astronomy, solar and planetary parameters, practical astronomical tables
works.purpose: An astronomical handbook with explanatory chapters and tables. This investigation is limited to its solar eccentricity and tropical-year values and a later table transmission claim.
works.date: The dossier does not assign a single composition date. The focused observation is dated by Mozaffari to Yazdigird year 251 (882/883 CE).

investigations.title: Solar eccentricity and year length in al-Battānī's zīj
investigations.field: Astronomy / mathematical astronomy / history of astronomy
investigations.historicalProblem: What solar parameters does modern specialist research report from al-Battānī's zīj, how do their historical model and sexagesimal units work, and what can be said about their later reception without mistaking an inferred table value for a modern physical parameter?
investigations.historicalContext: The zīj belongs to the Ptolemaic geocentric tradition. Mozaffari compares recorded and recomputed values for medieval solar models and distinguishes a parameter's formal historical value from modern reinterpretation. Van Dalen describes a full 57-chapter-and-tables witness in Escorial árabe 908, copied in the 12th or 13th century. Nothaft traces the value implicit in the Toledan Tables to al-Battānī. The dossier has not directly checked the Arabic text, Nallino's apparatus, or that manuscript.
investigations.method: Read Mozaffari's Table 1 and note 3 for the reported values and observation year; read Van Dalen's BEA entry for the work and surviving-witness context; read Nothaft's discussion and note 12 for the later Toledan value and exact Nallino page locators. Independently convert the sexagesimal year fraction and use the Ptolemaic relation qmax=arcsin(e/60) as a rounded arithmetic check. Keep secondary claims distinct from a fresh primary-text reading.
investigations.observationsOrCalculations: Mozaffari reports e=2;4,45 parts for a deferent radius of 60. In decimal units this is 2 + 4/60 + 45/3600 = 2.0791667 parts, or 0.0346528 of the radius. The Ptolemaic relation gives qmax≈1.9858555°, or about 1°59′9.1″, close to the rounded 1°59′10″ reported in the table tradition. Mozaffari gives the year as 365;14,26 days: 14/60 + 26/3600 day equals 5 hours, 46 minutes, 24 seconds. These checks validate conversions only; they do not confirm the source reading or the accuracy of the medieval observation.
investigations.reportedResult: The consulted secondary studies report that al-Battānī's zīj used a Ptolemaic solar eccentricity of 2;4,45 (radius 60) and a year length of 365;14,26 days. Nothaft identifies qmax=1;59,10° in the Toledan Tables as a value tracing back to al-Battānī. The values are historically meaningful parameters within their own model and tables.
investigations.whatWasNew: This case makes the value's historical units, model, observation-era locator, year conversion, and later table connection explicit. It makes no claim that al-Battānī invented solar eccentricity measurement, that a value in one model is identical to a Keplerian eccentricity, or that the observation has been independently remeasured from a manuscript.
investigations.limitations: The Arabic scan's title page and bibliographic metadata were checked, but the numerical Arabic and Latin passages and Nallino's apparatus were not yet collated directly in this research pass. Mozaffari's account is the immediate source for the reported observation and numerical values; Nothaft's article supplies secondary evidence for the Toledan transmission link. The arithmetic calculation from e=2;4,45 gives a qmax about one arcsecond below the rounded 1;59,10 value; this small difference is retained rather than silently forced to equality. No modern accuracy score, instrument reconstruction, or priority claim is inferred.
investigations.laterInfluence: Nothaft reports that the Toledan Tables' qmax=1;59,10° implies e=2;4,45 and traces that parameter back to al-Battānī. Van Dalen documents further translations and later users of the zīj, but this dossier does not assert that each named astronomer used this particular parameter without a passage-level check.

claims.text: The scanned Nallino title page identifies Pars III as containing the Arabic text of al-Battānī's zīj and dates that part to 1899; Van Dalen locates Chapter 28 in the Arabic volume at pp. 64–73, separately from its Latin translation in Pars I, pp. 43–48.

claims.uncertainty: The page range is a scholarly locator; the relevant Arabic chapter has not yet been collated directly in the scan.

claims.text: Van Dalen's biographical entry identifies al-Battānī as an astronomer from Harran, born before 858 and dead near Samarra in 929.
claims.locator: BEA entry, heading and opening biography
claims.uncertainty: These dates are the reference entry's reported bounds and are not independently harmonized against Arabic biographical notices here.

claims.text: Van Dalen reports that al-Battānī conducted observations at Raqqa during 877–918 CE.
claims.locator: BEA entry, observatory and instruments paragraph
claims.uncertainty: The chronology is reported by the biographical entry; individual observations and instruments require a separate primary-text audit.

claims.text: Van Dalen describes the Ṣābiʾ Zīj as surviving completely, with 57 chapters and tables, in Escorial árabe 908, a 12th- or 13th-century copy.
claims.locator: BEA entry, discussion of the Ṣābiʾ Zīj's witnesses and Nallino edition
claims.uncertainty: The manuscript itself and its catalogue record have not been inspected in this batch; the witness date is not the composition date.

claims.text: Mozaffari's Table 1 dates the al-Battānī observation to Yazdigird year 251, 15 April 882–14 April 883; note 3 says the solar observations were made after 882 CE.
claims.locator: Printed p. 323, Table 1 row 3; p. 329, note 3
claims.uncertainty: This is the date as reconstructed in the modern article; the underlying dated text has not been collated here.

claims.text: Mozaffari reports al-Battānī's Ptolemaic solar eccentricity as 2;4,45 parts on a radius of 60 and associates it with qmax=1;59,10°.
claims.uncertainty: The notation is a historical parameter in the Ptolemaic eccentric-circle model, not a direct measurement of modern Keplerian orbital eccentricity; the source text has not been collated.

claims.text: Van Dalen reports that Chapter 28 derives e=2;4,45 and that accurate calculation leads to qmax=1;59,10°, while the dossier's independent arcsin(e/60) computation yields 1;59,9.08°.
claims.locator: Van Dalen, p. 398 and n. 81; dossier calculation in observationsOrCalculations
claims.uncertainty: The difference is under one arcsecond and may involve rounding, precision, or the historical derivation, but this has not been established. The Arabic text and calculation steps remain to be checked.

claims.text: Converting 2;4,45 to 2.0791667 and applying qmax=arcsin(e/60) gives about 1°59′9.1″, close to the rounded 1°59′10″ value reported by the secondary sources.
claims.locator: Independent arithmetic check using the model described in Mozaffari, pp. 314–315, and the reported value at p. 329, note 3
claims.uncertainty: The calculation checks normalized modern arithmetic from the reported sexagesimal value, not the manuscript reading or the rounding convention in the historical table.

claims.text: Mozaffari reports a tropical-year value of 365;14,26 days, equivalent by sexagesimal conversion to 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes, 24 seconds.
claims.locator: Printed p. 329, note 3; conversion independently recomputed here
claims.uncertainty: The conversion is arithmetic; the underlying edition and year-length derivation have not been directly checked.

claims.text: The reported value 2;4,45 is expressed in the Ptolemaic solar eccentric-circle model and must not be presented as numerically identical to the modern Keplerian eccentricity of Earth's orbit.
claims.uncertainty: A conversion between the two models requires stating the modelling assumptions; this dossier does not make a modern-accuracy comparison.

claims.text: Nothaft identifies the Toledan Tables' qmax=1;59,10° as implying e=2;4,45 and traces this parameter back to al-Battānī.
claims.locator: Nothaft, p. 148 and p. 155 n. 12; the note points to Nallino, vol. 1, pp. 43–48 (chapter 28) and vol. 2, pp. 78–83
claims.uncertainty: This is a specialist's reported textual transmission link; the Toledan manuscripts and cited Nallino pages were not independently checked here.

claims.text: The evidence in this batch supports one specific Toledan Tables transmission link; it does not prove direct use of the same parameter by every later astronomer named in general accounts of the zīj's reception.
claims.locator: Nothaft, p. 148; Van Dalen, BEA entry on transmission and later readers
claims.uncertainty: A broader influence history needs a separate chain of dated manuscripts, tables, translations, or explicit citations.
